name: Hamptons diet

card.summary: A celebrity-associated low-carbohydrate, higher-protein eating plan with a Mediterranean twist that people follow to lose body fat and look leaner.
card.note: Nutritionists have raised concerns about fibre and micronutrient intake in some versions of the plan.

quick.overview:
The Hamptons Diet is a weight-loss plan set out in a 2004 book by New York physician Fred Pescatore, formerly medical director of the Atkins Center. It combines lower carbohydrates and plenty of protein with Mediterranean-style fats such as olive and macadamia nut oil.

The appearance payoff people seek is leaner body composition: less body fat, a more defined face and midsection. The diet drew attention in 2004 through celebrity and fashion press coverage.
quick.how: Followers build meals around lean meat and fish, vegetables and monounsaturated fats, and limit refined carbohydrates. The book provides 30 days of meal plans and a large set of recipes, with macadamia nut oil a signature ingredient.
quick.risks: Dietitians quoted in encyclopedia accounts say some menus provide little fibre, vitamin C, calcium, folate, vitamin D and vitamin E, and that fat can supply up to 70 percent of calories. No clinical trial of the diet itself has been published in mainstream journals. People with medical conditions usually discuss any major diet change with a clinician.

lead: The Hamptons Diet is a low-carbohydrate eating plan described in the 2004 book The Hamptons Diet: Lose Weight Quickly and Safely with the Doctor's Delicious Meal Plans by Fred Pescatore, published by Wiley.[1]

It is intended to lower body fat, which people pursue to look leaner. It combines Atkins-style carbohydrate restriction with Mediterranean features: lean proteins and monounsaturated fats, especially macadamia nut oil.[1][2]

The plan became a topic in celebrity and fashion magazines, and nutrition writers have commented on its fibre and micronutrient content. No clinical trials of the Hamptons Diet itself have been reported in mainstream research journals.[2]

chain: Lower calorie intake and body-weight loss
angle.text: Followers use it to lose body fat and appear leaner, which makes facial structure and muscle definition more visible. Its approach follows the broader low-carbohydrate pattern of reducing weight through changed food choices.

paras: Pescatore's book presents a weight-loss plan inspired by the Atkins and Mediterranean approaches, with healthy carbohydrates and ample protein aimed at a low-glycemic balance, plus 30 days of meal plans and many recipes.[1] Reviews note that he differs from Atkins mainly in the type and amount of fats he recommends, favouring monounsaturated fats.[2]
Typical foods include chicken, fish and other lean meats, with saturated-fat foods allowed in moderation.[2]

Pescatore is a Manhattan-based internist and nutrition author who served as medical director of Robert Atkins's Atkins Medical Center from 1994 to 1999 and opened Partners in Integrative Medicine in 2003.[2] His other books include Feed Your Kids Well (1998) and Thin for Good.[2]

Nutritionists cited in encyclopedia entries have said some versions give limited fibre, vitamin C, calcium, folate, vitamin D and vitamin E, and that fat can reach up to 70 percent of calories in some menus.[2] Clinical dietitian Shweta Rastogi lists it among fad diets, and dietitian Sue Baic has said it places unnecessary emphasis on carbohydrate cutting and relies on expensive foods.[2]
Readers and reviewers also note that recipes can be costly or time-consuming.[2] The diet was widely covered in celebrity and fashion magazines.[2]

No studies found. Published reviews of the diet state that no clinical trials of the Hamptons Diet have appeared in mainstream journals; the broader category of low-carbohydrate diets has been studied separately.[2]

timeline.event: Pescatore becomes medical director of the Atkins Medical Center (to 1999).[2]
The Hamptons Diet is published by Wiley on 29 April 2004.[1]
A Wiley paperback edition is released.[1]
